target: AG1’s claim that Election Day should be a national holiday because it removes workday scheduling barriers for voters
objection: A federal holiday does not automatically give private-sector workers paid time off, so the people most constrained by work schedules—especially low-income retail and service workers—may still have to work and gain little real voting access from the holiday label alone.

target: AG1’s assumption that a holiday is the best way to raise turnout
objection: An election-day holiday by itself is not a proven or reliable turnout strategy; targeted reforms like legally enforceable time off to vote and automatic voter registration are more directly tied to removing barriers.

target: AG2’s claim that a national holiday fails to help low-wage workers because employers need not close or provide paid leave
objection: Even without universal paid leave, holiday status would still reduce scheduling constraints in practice by closing many employers and government offices or reducing hours, and it could be paired with workplace time-off protections instead of being treated as an either/or choice.

target: AG1’s reply that a holiday would still help low-wage workers by reducing schedules and could be paired with protections
objection: Workers in sectors that stay open on holidays—such as healthcare, transit, retail, food service, and other essential services—would still need to work or swap shifts, so holiday status does not guarantee real voting time and may also worsen polling-place lines by concentrating voting on one day.

target: AG2’s claim that a holiday leaves low-wage workers effectively unchanged and increases lines
objection: A national Election Day holiday can be enacted together with an enforceable paid voting-time requirement, which directly addresses low-wage workers, and election administrators can plan for higher demand so the holiday need not create chaos.

target: AG1’s framing that a holiday can be combined with paid voting time to solve the main problem
objection: If a holiday only works when another enforceable workplace rule is added, then the holiday is redundant at best and could distract from or delay the more targeted reforms that actually ensure access.

target: AG2’s redundancy argument and claim that targeted reforms are better than a holiday
objection: A national holiday is not a substitute for access reforms; it is a nationwide baseline that reduces scheduling pressure across schools, government offices, and many employers, and it can be implemented alongside broader reforms rather than instead of them.

target: AG1’s claim that the holiday helps by reducing scheduling pressure nationwide
objection: Election operations depend on staffing and local capacity, so a federal holiday can create mismatches and bottlenecks if polling places, election workers, and contractors face reduced availability; that makes it a weaker lever than enforceable worker time-off rules and administrative reforms.

target: AG2’s claim that holiday logistics make the policy unstable and inferior to targeted reforms
objection: Many countries already hold elections on weekends or holidays, which shows that holiday-based election timing is feasible, and a national holiday also provides a uniform baseline that avoids patchwork state-by-state voting-time rules.

target: AG1’s appeal to international precedent and a nationwide baseline
objection: Other countries using holidays does not show that a holiday by itself improves turnout in the United States, and a uniform calendar day can still be unequal in practice if low-wage workers remain scheduled to work or lack real paid time off.

target: AG2’s claim that only enforceable worker time-off rules matter and that holiday precedent does not prove turnout gains
objection: A national Election Day holiday is the most direct way to overcome scheduling constraints and the most workable nationwide first step, because it can be adopted across the country more easily than employer-by-employer rules and gives people a non-workday baseline for voting.

target: AG1’s claim that a holiday is the most workable nationwide first step
objection: A national holiday could become the headline reform that crowds out more effective measures such as enforceable paid voting time and administrative streamlining, so it may consume legislative bandwidth without solving the core access problem for workers.

target: AG2’s opportunity-cost argument that a holiday would crowd out targeted reforms
objection: A national holiday is not a substitute for those reforms but a system-wide baseline that removes scheduling conflicts for schools, workplaces, and childcare arrangements, and the legislation can be structured as a package including both the holiday and enforceable access protections.

target: AG1’s package approach and claim that the holiday helps families and schools
objection: Even if some institutions close, a holiday can shift more coverage and strain onto hourly workers in sectors that remain open, making scheduling harder for the very people who already struggle to vote unless enforceable paid leave is actually in place.

target: AG2’s claim that holiday status can worsen shift pressure for open workplaces
objection: That concern only applies if the policy is holiday-only; if Election Day is made a national holiday as part of an enforceable package protecting paid time to vote, then the holiday changes incentives and removes the shift-pressure problem AG2 describes.

target: AG1’s package-based defense of the holiday
objection: If the real solution is enforceable paid voting time, then the holiday becomes unnecessary symbolism and administrative cost, and international precedent does not prove the holiday itself causes turnout gains in the United States.

target: AG2’s claim that the package makes the holiday nonessential and that precedent does not prove impact
objection: A holiday helps make enforceable paid voting time workable in practice by reducing ordinary scheduling pressure on schools, employers, and households, so the holiday is not merely symbolic but improves the chance that the legal right translates into actual time to vote.

target: AG1’s claim that the holiday makes enforceable voting-time rights more usable
objection: The operational mechanism is enforceable worker time to vote, not the calendar; if the right still depends on employer scheduling and coverage decisions, the holiday is largely redundant and does not reliably protect workers from shift pressure or lost wages.

target: AG2’s redundancy argument
objection: Even a legal right to vote-time still has to be invoked by workers, while a national holiday reduces the need to request exceptions, swap shifts, or fear retaliation, making the right easier to use in practice.

target: AG1’s claim that a holiday reduces the need for workers to invoke their rights
objection: Research shows an election holiday by itself is not an effective turnout strategy compared with other voting-access reforms, so policymakers should prioritize enforceable paid voting time and administrative access measures instead of centering a calendar change.

target: AG2’s claim that a holiday is weaker than enforceable time-to-vote rules
objection: The criticism sets an unfair standard by judging the holiday only “by itself”; a national holiday directly removes the day-of scheduling barrier in a simple, nationwide way that is more straightforward than employer-by-employer enforcement, while still allowing paid voting-time protections to be added.

target: AG1’s claim that a holiday is a simpler baseline than targeted enforcement
objection: A holiday may be simpler, but it is not the more reliable way to give working voters usable time; employer time-off protections and expanded voting access across more days or hours directly address whether people can vote without losing wages or dealing with shift pressure.

target: AG2’s claim that enforceable time-to-vote rules are the only reliable fix
objection: A national holiday reduces the need to request leave or negotiate shift swaps, standardizing the day as non-routine and making it more likely workers have automatic availability to vote without stigma or retaliation.

target: AG1’s claim that a holiday standardizes the day and reduces request pressure
objection: A single Election Day holiday creates a one-day peak that can stress employers and polling places, while it still leaves workers needing guaranteed protected time across the broader period they may need for childcare, transportation, and schedule coordination.

target: AG2’s concern that a holiday creates a peak and ignores broader timing needs
objection: Election administrators can plan for higher demand with staffing and logistics, and the holiday still solves the central day-of scheduling clash that many workers and caregivers face when they are most likely to vote.
